/politics/2026/nov/20/burnham-trade-yout.headline: What exactly is in the deal between the UK and the EU?
/politics/2026/nov/20/burnham-trade-yout.excerpt: After months of on-off negotiations, leaks and late nights, the EU and UK have agreed a 12-page statement setting out the next steps in their relationship. What exactly have they agreed? The three deals The two sides have struck three deals long expected from this summit: food and drink, emissions trading and a youth exchange programme. The food and drink deal will ease Brexit controls on the vast majority of animal and plant products being traded between Britain and the EU, a boon for producers of meat, dairy, wine and flowers among many other products. If all goes well – and there is still an if – the deal will apply from 1 March 2028. The energy deal relinks the British and EU emissions trading schemes, shielding industrial producers on both sides from levies on polluting products, such as steel and fertilisers, as well as electricity. This should enter into force in 2028. Under the youth experience scheme, up to 100,000 British people each year would be able to live, work, travel and study in the EU for up to three years. The same number of young Europeans would be able to come to the UK. Young people should be able to take advantage of the scheme by 2030 at the latest.
/politics/2026/nov/20/burnham-trade-yout.trail: The two sides have come to agreements on food and drink, emissions trading and the youth exchange scheme

/politics/2026/nov/20/burnham-trade-yout.headline: Burnham has agreed EU reset deal with tuition fees issue unresolved, says No 10
/politics/2026/nov/20/burnham-trade-yout.excerpt: The UK and EU have agreed a reset deal, Downing Street has said, although the level of tuition fees EU students will pay to study at UK universities remains unresolved. “The deal is done – negotiations have concluded,” a No 10 statement said, less than an hour after the prime minister, Andy Burnham, arrived at the summit venue in Brussels, where he was greeted by Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, and António Costa, the European Council president. The reset means there is agreement on three deals – food and drink, emissions trading, and a youth mobility scheme – but EU sources say these deals will not enter into force unless the UK reaches a settlement with the bloc over tuition fee rates for European students. The statement came shortly after headlines on Friday suggested that the tuition fee issue could cause other parts of the process to collapse. However, after the deal was announced, UK officials pushed back strongly against the idea that the three plans could be jeopardised by a failure to agree on tuition fees, saying the issues were completely separate. Earlier, EU officials had indicated that progress on the main deals would be contingent on tuition fees. While talks on tuition fees are scheduled to last another six months, the officials said new arrangements for food and agriculture would come into force in March 2028 regardless of an agreement on the issue.
/politics/2026/nov/20/burnham-trade-yout.trail: Discord between EU and UK on whether arrangements for food and drink, emissions trading and youth mobility scheme depend on settlement for students

/politics/2026/nov/20/burnham-trade-yout.headline: Senior Tories urge Badenoch to drop Brexit talk in major strategy shift, sources say
/politics/2026/nov/20/burnham-trade-yout.excerpt: Kemi Badenoch has been advised by her team to limit the amount of time she spends discussing Brexit and Europe, the Guardian has been told, moving the Conservatives away from an issue that defined the party for many years. While the Tory leader still gives views on Brexit – in an opinion piece in the Daily Mail on Thursday she condemned Andy Burnham’s ongoing reset with the EU as a “backwards” move – sources say it is now seen as a second-order subject. Instead, Badenoch intends to focus on areas the party believes are more fertile electoral ground, in particular the economy, the cost of social security and defence. One source said Badenoch had been advised to shift the narrative away from Brexit by Stephen Gilbert, a former Conservative official who is now a peer and who joined the Tory leader’s team as a senior political adviser a year ago. Although another party source said Gilbert’s advice was “more nuanced” than this, Badenoch’s recent run of speeches and interventions appears to demonstrate the change. In eight sets of prime minister’s questions since Burnham entered No 10 over the summer, Badenoch and her deputy, Alex Burghart, who took one session when Burnham was away, have focused on Europe just once, on 28 October, when she challenged the PM on whether or not he wanted a new Brexit referendum.
/politics/2026/nov/20/burnham-trade-yout.trail: Exclusive: While PM pushes for EU reset, Tory leader is moving away from ‘divisive’ issue that defined party for years

/politics/2026/nov/20/burnham-trade-yout.headline: What impact has Brexit had on the UK and EU economies?
/politics/2026/nov/20/burnham-trade-yout.excerpt: The UK and EU will hold the second summit since Brexit on Friday against a volatile economic backdrop. Taking place in Brussels as the war in the Middle East hits the global economy, the prime minister, Andy Burnham, will meet the head of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, and the president of the European Council, António Costa. Burnham has said that Brexit “has not worked”, citing damage to the UK economy from leaving the bloc. However, there are also economic challenges facing the EU. Here we spell out the economic context behind the talks. How has the UK fared since Brexit? After the 2016 Brexit vote, years of political turmoil and economic uncertainty damaged business investment. Trade has also been hit by new barriers and red tape for exporters under the Brexit deal agreed by Boris Johnson. Analysis by the economist Nick Bloom shows that UK GDP per head is between 6% and 8% lower than it would have been without Brexit. The Office for Budget Responsibility estimates a 4% hit over a 15-year period. UK services trade has fared better. UK goods exports to the EU in 2025 were 14% below 2019 in real terms. Exports outside the EU were 8% lower. Services exports were 28% higher to the EU and 26% higher elsewhere, fuelled by Britain’s dominant financial services sector, as well as travel, accountancy, law, professional services, telecommunications and IT. Britain has conducted trade policy independently of Brussels since Brexit.
/politics/2026/nov/20/burnham-trade-yout.trail: As talks are held in Brussels over closer relations, we examine the economic context and the challenges ahead

/uk-news/2026/nov/20/far-right-activist-.headline: Woman raped by strangers after being drugged by husband calls for consent law changes
/uk-news/2026/nov/20/far-right-activist-.excerpt: A woman who was raped by strangers after being drugged by her husband has warned of “serious questions about how the law deals with consent”, as four men who abused her were convicted on Thursday. Philip Young, 50, advertised his then wife, Joanne Young, on dating and swinging websites, presenting it as a “kink” for both of them, Winchester crown court heard. In fact, he had been sedating her, plunging her into an “inanimate state” in which anything could be done to her by the men who answered the adverts, jurors were told. The former Conservative councillor pleaded guilty earlier in the year to dozens of charges of abuse against his former wife, who has waived her right to anonymity. On Thursday, Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32; Richard Wilkins, 62; Norman Macksoni, 48; and Mohammed Hassan, 38, were convicted of various offences against Joanne Young after a three-week trial. The case has drawn comparisons to that of Gisèle Pelicot, who was drugged by her husband and raped by dozens of strangers in France. It can now be revealed that Wiltshire police received advice from the Pelicot investigators on how to approach their inquiries. The Crown Prosecution Service said it was the first time a jury had convicted multiple defendants relating to organised drug-facilitated sexual assault in England. After the verdicts, Wiltshire police said that although rare, the true scale of drug-facilitated sexual offences in the UK could be significantly underreported.
/uk-news/2026/nov/20/far-right-activist-.trail: Four men convicted of sexual assault and rape of Joanne Young, whose husband advertised her on UK swinging websites

/uk-news/2026/nov/20/far-right-activist-.headline: ‘Silence is not an option’: Joanne Young makes statement outside court
/uk-news/2026/nov/20/far-right-activist-.excerpt: After the conviction of four men for sexually assaulting and raping her at the invitation of her husband, Philip Young, Joanne Young – who waived her anonymity before the prosecution – read a statement outside Winchester crown court. In it, she reflected on her belief that the case held a wider message about how the law deals with consent, and what the prosecution might mean for other women who are the victims of abuse by men. “The guilty result today is a relief, and it’s a relief not just for me and my family, but a relief for what this means for other women in the future. “It means that those who find themselves facing what I have are more likely to come forward, and more likely to have faith in the criminal justice system. “More broadly for women and girls who have been abused by men, it sends the message that you can be believed and understood. “Knowing what has happened to me without my knowledge or consent has been incredibly difficult to process, and this abuse has cost me my life as I knew it. “The person I trusted most in the world betrayed me in the most horrific way. This has resulted in a devastating impact on the lives of myself and my children. “What happened to me was not the act of one man alone. Others were invited to take part, and they chose to. That choice makes them complicit in what was done to me, and today’s verdicts recognise that. “But this case also raises serious questions about how the law deals with consent.
/uk-news/2026/nov/20/far-right-activist-.trail: After conviction of her abusers, Young says her case raises questions about how the law deals with consent

/uk-news/2026/nov/20/far-right-activist-.headline: Spiked nightcaps and invitations to strangers: how Philip Young sexually abused his wife for 15 years
/uk-news/2026/nov/20/far-right-activist-.excerpt: When Philip Young served as a Conservative party councillor for Swindon council, his contemporaries viewed him as a perfectly normal family man with “no edge to him”. But behind closed doors he orchestrated a systematic campaign of abuse against his then wife, Joanne Young, secretly administering sedatives to render her unconscious, disoriented and amnesiac. Over a period of at least 15 years, he and other men raped and sexually assaulted her in her own bed at their home in Swindon. The father of three pleaded guilty to more than 50 offences, including drugging, raping and sexually assaulting Joanne, who has been praised for her bravery in waiving her anonymity. His co-accused Connor Sanderson-Doyle, Richard Wilkins, Norman Macksoni and Mohammed Hassan were convicted on Thursday by a jury of their involvement. Another man, Dean Hamilton, pleaded guilty in February to rape. The high-profile case has drawn comparisons to the Gisèle Pelicot trial in France, and it can now be revealed that the Crown Prosecution Service and Wiltshire police met the French team of investigators and prosecutors for advice. Testimony and police interviews paint a picture of a carefully maintained domestic facade masking a predatory reality. Joanne, who was married to Young for 20 years and had been with him since 2002, described their relationship as traditionally monogamous and her own preferences as strictly “vanilla”.
/uk-news/2026/nov/20/far-right-activist-.trail: Joanne Young, who has waived anonymity, was subjected to years of drugging and rape by former Swindon councillor, who invited other men to assault her

/uk-news/2026/nov/20/far-right-activist-.headline: Lawyer calls for urgent review of Letby convictions after expert witness revelations
/uk-news/2026/nov/20/far-right-activist-.excerpt: Lucy Letby’s lawyer has said the court of appeal must urgently review her convictions, after it was revealed that a key medical witness in the prosecution’s case was barred from treating patients because of safety concerns. The Guardian revealed this week that Prof Peter Hindmarsh – a crucial expert witness who provided an opinion at Letby’s trial that two babies had been poisoned with insulin – was excluded from clinical practice in March 2023 because his hospital considered him unsafe to treat children in relation to insulin. The jury in the case were never told of the restriction placed on Hindmarsh, who was described by the prosecution in court as “the pre-eminent expert” on insulin. Letby’s lawyer Mark McDonald, who has applied to the miscarriages of justice watchdog, the Criminal Cases Review Commission, for Letby’s convictions to be referred back to the court of appeal, said: “These revelations about Prof Hindmarsh, and the failure to disclose material information about him to the defence at trial, raise fundamental questions, and it is more urgent than ever that the court of appeal re-examines the safety of all Lucy Letby’s convictions. “She is an innocent woman in prison, serving whole-life sentences, yet material information that could have been of critical importance to her defence was not disclosed. Did the police know? How did this information remain undisclosed? “We need answers. Lucy deserves answers.
/uk-news/2026/nov/20/far-right-activist-.trail: Failure to disclose Peter Hindmarsh’s exclusion from practice raises ‘fundamental questions’ over nurse’s case

/uk-news/2026/nov/20/far-right-activist-.headline: Member of anti-migrant group found guilty of Staffordshire murder
/uk-news/2026/nov/20/far-right-activist-.excerpt: A member of anti-migrant group Raise the Colours has been found guilty of murdering a man in a “completely unprovoked and unjustified” attack. Billy Allison, 36, delivered a “very, very hard” punch with the “stance and skill of an experienced fighter” which killed 44-year-old Matthew O’Gara while he was on a night out in Lichfield on 24 May. A jury of seven men and five women were not told of Allison’s link to Raise the Colours, which has been responsible for hanging hundreds of union jack flags on lamp-posts and roundabouts across the country, during the trial at Stafford crown court. Allison was also found guilty of grievous bodily harm with intent on Wednesday for twice punching O’Gara’s friend, 62-year-old Adam Cooper, on the same night as the murder, leaving him with a fractured eye socket and nose. O’Gara’s family thanked the emergency services who cared for him and said he remained “deeply loved” and “will always hold a special place in our hearts”. “While the conclusion of the court proceedings has brought a measure of justice, it can never replace the loss we have suffered or bring Matthew back,” they said in a statement. The trial heard how Allison had been drinking and had taken cocaine before he attacked the two men – neither of whom he knew. He had spent the day with his partner, Charlotte Dean, and fellow Raise the Colours members Ryan Bridge and Ben Cullen and their partners.
/uk-news/2026/nov/20/far-right-activist-.trail: Raise the Colours activist Billy Allison, 36, killed man in ‘completely unprovoked and unjustified’ attack, say police

/business/2026/nov/20/global-stock-marke.headline: Anthropic’s historic stock market debut: key takeaways, and what comes next for the AI industry
/business/2026/nov/20/global-stock-marke.excerpt: In the end, Anthropic’s much-anticipated IPO more than lived up to the hype. The market’s embrace of one of the AI industry’s most talked about companies has resulted in the maker of the Claude chatbot becoming one of the world’s most valuable firms after just one day of trading. With many of the company’s founders, investors and employees now worth billions of dollars – and demand for the company’s stock remaining resilient – attention now turns to the stability of the wider market, and the global headwinds that experts say could threaten the AI industry over the coming months. Here’s a rundown of what we can gather after a big day for Anthropic and the AI industry Biggest IPO in history, but it’s not all good news Closing the day about 17% higher than its initial public offering price, Anthropic shares were trading at just over $97 when the market closed taking its valuation to roughly $1.7tn. The share price initially soared by 34% when trading got under way on Thursday, briefly taking the company’s valuation to more than $2tn. The blockbuster debut easily places the IPO as the biggest in history, with the 980m shares sold raising $81bn, surpassing the previous record held by Elon Musk’s SpaceX’s $75bn raised in June. Despite the excitement, major US stock indexes fells to seven-month lows on Thursday, dragged down by growing concerns about the longer-term outlook for the AI industry.
/business/2026/nov/20/global-stock-marke.trail: A record breaking IPO has raised billions for the AI frontier lab – but experts say the coming months could prove bumpy, as the industry faces a variety of challenges

/business/2026/nov/20/global-stock-marke.headline: Anthropic closes first day of public trading at $1.3tn valuation after largest-ever IPO
/business/2026/nov/20/global-stock-marke.excerpt: Anthropic closed its first day of trading on the US stock market about 17% higher than its initial public offering price. At the close of market on Thursday, Anthropic shares were trading at just over $97 with a nearly $1.3tn total market capitalization, $1.75tn fully diluted. While the final share value was higher than the IPO price of $83, it marked a dip from an early high of $111.50. The firm’s shares initially soared 34% when trading got under way on its US market debut on Thursday, valuing the company at more than $2tn. Nonetheless, Anthropic’s ranked among the biggest stock market flotations in history. The artificial intelligence startup, founded in 2021, became one of the most valuable publicly traded businesses in the world. “Today puts the company in a stronger financial position, and in doing so only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing,” said Anthropic’s chief executive, Dario Amodei, who rang the Nasdaq opening bell. Anthropic announced late on Wednesday that it had sold 980m shares to underwriters, an upsized offering that raised $81.3bn, surpassing the previous record set by SpaceX’s initial $75bn fundraise in June. US stocks slumped at the end of trading, a potential sign that Anthropic’s mammoth IPO wasn’t enough to alleviate concerns over the AI industry’s volatility. Most of the major chipmakers’ stock prices closed the day lower than they started.
/business/2026/nov/20/global-stock-marke.trail: AI startup and Claude chatbot maker became one of the world’s most valuable publicly traded businesses with final share price of $97

/business/2026/nov/20/global-stock-marke.headline: Who are Anthropic’s seven co-founders, now worth $180bn?
/business/2026/nov/20/global-stock-marke.excerpt: The paper fortunes of Anthropic’s seven co-founders reached a total of more than $180bn on Thursday as shares in their company started trading at a price ahead of expectations. The opening price of $111.50 (£85) per share valued the entrepreneurs’ stakes – including the chief executive, Dario Amodei, and his sister Daniela – at between $26.5bn and $27bn each. The founders have pledged to donate 80% of their shareholdings in Anthropic to philanthropic causes, which would equate to about $150bn at the current share price. Other investors generating considerable wealth from the float and the late share price surge include Madonna’s manager, Guy Oseary, whose venture capital firm, Sound Ventures, which he co-founded with Hollywood actor Ashton Kutcher, reportedly owns 0.5% as an early investor. That stake would be worth $10bn at the opening price. At the closing price of $97.17, the combined co-founders’ stakes had fallen in value to just over $160bn at around $23bn each. The Sound Ventures stake was worth about $8.75bn. Anthropic has also committed 5% of its shares to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, which will “explore large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations”. The company has said some of the proceeds could be used to address AI’s impact on the job market, though fears the technology will lead to significant job losses have yet to be realised.
/business/2026/nov/20/global-stock-marke.trail: The company counts physicists, a former journalist and an associate of the pope among its guiding lights

/business/2026/nov/20/global-stock-marke.headline: Anthropic sets share price at $83 for stock market debut, above expected range
/business/2026/nov/20/global-stock-marke.excerpt: Anthropic set the share price for its debut on the US stock market at $83 on Wednesday, positioning the artificial intelligence company for one of the biggest initial public offerings in history. The firm is slated to begin trading on Thursday under the ticker symbol ANT, with CEO Dario Amodei and other co-founders ringing the bell to open the Nasdaq exchange. The pricing is above Anthropic’s earlier estimates. Last week, the San Francisco-based company, founded in 2021, set its preliminary share price at $70 to $78. With all shares counted, those prices put Anthropic’s initial public offering (IPO) from $1.26tn to $1.41tn. Elon Musk’s SpaceX debuted on Wall Street in June with the biggest market offering ever at $1.77tn. With Anthropic setting its share price at $83, it could now surpass SpaceX. Amodei is planning to sell about $260m worth of shares with the IPO, as are his six fellow co-founders. At the top of the price range, the co-founders’ stakes will be worth more than $18bn each. When Anthropic filed for its IPO last month, the company detailed rapidly rising revenue in its prospectus: $41m in 2023, $386m in 2024, $4.585bn in 2025 (an increase of more than 1,000%), then $16.286bn in the first six months of 2026 alone. The company disclosed that, as of the end of June, it had raised $141.1bn. Despite the increasing revenue, Anthropic disclosed a net loss of $80bn for the first half of 2026.
/business/2026/nov/20/global-stock-marke.trail: Artificial intelligence firm positioned for one of the biggest IPOs in history, with trading slated to begin Thursday

/business/2026/nov/20/global-stock-marke.headline: Anthropic IPO: how can I buy shares, and is it worth it?
/business/2026/nov/20/global-stock-marke.excerpt: The technology company Anthropic is heading for a blockbuster stock market listing this week in what is slated to be one of the largest debuts in history. The company is a leader in artificial intelligence, and is best known for its chatbot Claude. The float, which is expected to value the business at $1.4tn (£1tn), comes at a volatile time for tech stocks, yet it has been reported that the shares could be six times oversubscribed. How much are the shares? When a company floats it issues a prospectus for would-be investors that details its activities and lays out the share offering, including an estimated price. Anthropic’s prospectus explains that the shares on sale will be 825m of class A common stock, and that the initial public offering (IPO) price will between $70 and $78 a share. However, the final price will be set on Wednesday. The shares will come with voting rights, but, if all the shares’ votes are combined they will only represent 49.9% of the total vote available, so will not allow buyers to be able to force any changes in the way the company is run. How do I buy shares? The shares will be listed on the Nasdaq in New York on Thursday, and will be available to individual investors alongside big institutions. In the UK, several investment platforms are offering customers the chance to subscribe to shares, including AJ Bell, Hargreaves Lansdown, Robinhood and eToro.
/business/2026/nov/20/global-stock-marke.trail: Stock market debut of Claude AI chatbot maker is expected to be one of the biggest flotations in history

/uk-news/2026/nov/20/friday-cold-weather.headline: What is the polar vortex, why has it flipped and will it bring snow?
/uk-news/2026/nov/20/friday-cold-weather.excerpt: The polar vortex has flipped direction, signalling the earliest “major sudden stratospheric warming” ever observed. We examine how it is likely to affect you and whether it will bring snow. What is the polar vortex? It is a circle of strong winds in the stratosphere, about six to 30 miles (10 to 50km) above the surface of the Earth, that usually blow in a west to east direction around the Arctic, creating an insulating ring between the cold air mass closer to the north pole and warmer air further south. What happens when it changes direction? The vortex relocates or splits in two, which allows cold air from high altitudes and the pole to spill down over northern Europe, north America, Siberia, Japan and other parts of east Asia. Why is it happening now? This part of the stratosphere is thought to have warmed by up to 50C in just a couple of days as a result of large atmospheric waves spreading up from the troposphere, the lowest and densest layer of Earth’s atmosphere. Hang on, a warmer stratosphere is going to usher in cooler surface temperatures? Not always, but in this case, yes, for at least some parts of the northern hemisphere in the coming weeks. Is this a problem? The polar vortex is part of the climate system. Any disruption has knock-on effects. In the north Atlantic, for example, it upsets the jet stream and weather patterns for millions of people. How does it affect the weather?
/uk-news/2026/nov/20/friday-cold-weather.trail: We look at what is happening over the Arctic and what it might mean for winter weather in the northern hemisphere

/football/2026/nov/20/harry-kane-ankle-l.headline: Ballon d’Or winner Harry Kane signs new contract with Bayern through to 2029
/football/2026/nov/20/harry-kane-ankle-l.excerpt: England captain and Ballon d’Or winner Harry Kane has signed a new deal with Bayern Munich through to 2029, the German club have announced. Kane moved to Bayern from Tottenham in 2023 for a record €100m fee and has proved a huge success, scoring 156 goals in 161 competitive appearances and leading the German club to two Bundesliga titles and a DFB Cup. The 33-year-old was named as the world’s best male player last week after scoring a remarkable 89 goals for club and country since the start of August 2025, becoming the first Englishman to win the Ballon d’Or in 25 years and the first Bayern player since Karl-Heinz Rummenigge in 1981 to win the award. “I feel right at home at FC Bayern,” said Kane. “I love the club, the fans and the city of Munich. We have a fantastic team and, in Vincent Kompany, a fantastic manager. It makes me very proud to be part of this club. My whole family is very happy here. I was keen to stay. I’m now looking forward to the future and I want to win many more titles with this great club.” In September, Kane became the fastest player in German history to reach 100 Bundesliga goals, doing so in 98 games to shatter the previous record set by Dieter Mueller in 1977 by 31 games. Bayern did not disclose ⁠financial details of the agreement. However, German media reported that the extension is the most lucrative contract in the club’s history and part of a long-term commitment to the England captain.
/football/2026/nov/20/harry-kane-ankle-l.trail: England captain and Ballon d’Or winner Harry Kane has signed a new deal with Bayern Munich through to 2029, the German club have announced

/football/2026/nov/20/harry-kane-ankle-l.headline: Harry Kane’s Ballon d’Or party gives way to anxiety-filled hangover for Bayern Munich
/football/2026/nov/20/harry-kane-ankle-l.excerpt: It was the moment they had all been … not so much waiting for, but planning, pushing and yearning for. In the videos that announce the starting lineup on the giant scoreboard before kick-off, every Bayern Munich player turns to face the camera with their personal salute, greeting or goal celebration, the playful progression from the standard folding of arms. Except on Saturday evening, the No 9 turned around smiling, and cradling the golden trophy. In the midweek DFB Pokal stroll against Magdeburg there had been a salute, the players welcoming Harry Kane on to the pitch with a guard of honour to commemorate his Ballon d’Or victory two nights before. This, however, was the real party, the moment where the England captain’s and Bayern’s successful union and the apex it has reached was celebrated in front of a global audience. There was every reason to believe it would be a full and satisfying victory lap, even in Der Klassiker, with proper competition so often bringing the best out of the Rekordmeister. Dortmund, however, did not read the script. Neither did the football gods. Kane was not completely neutered in this and laid on yet another assist, nodding across goal to present Dayot Upamecano a second goal in successive Bundesliga games That looked like the winner until Fábio Silva’s 89th-minute equaliser for the visitors. Yet in between, there was frustration for the man who has walked on water since arriving in Munich.
/football/2026/nov/20/harry-kane-ankle-l.trail: Dortmund did not read the script, remaining level on points with the defending champions at the top of the table

/football/2026/nov/20/harry-kane-ankle-l.headline: Team success, the ‘Bundesliga tax’ and the World Cup: three takeaways from the 2026 Ballon d’Or
/football/2026/nov/20/harry-kane-ankle-l.excerpt: It was an awards show that, as Michael Owen admitted, could have been a phone call – as it was in 2001 when he won. A quarter-century on, a ballroom full of footballers, power brokers, a gravity-defying dancer and a handful of heckling rabble-rousers plodded through a three-hour slog of a ceremony. Aside from a reminder to viewers at home just how precious our free time is, what could be gleaned from the men’s element of the Ballon d’Or ceremony? It’s hard to stand out in a team game As early voting for the midterms progresses in the United States, the party affiliation of a candidate carries as much weight as their name. This year, as with many this century, the panel of voters were similarly interested in team performance beyond individual accomplishments. Not to say that Harry Kane didn’t make a strong individual case to win. The presumptive frontrunner this year, Kane also took home the honor as top men’s striker of the year roughly 45 minutes before the top prize went his way. Scoring 64 goals in 56 club matches is staggering. So, too, is his growing reputation as a world-class chance creator with the through balls he threads with increasing ease. Kane stands out as a stat-accumulator in a waning era of meticulous systems, and his gilded peers playing for teams operating off such intricate models were largely held back. Premier League-winning Arsenal also reached the Champions League final, yet none of their players ranked higher than 15th (Declan Rice).
/football/2026/nov/20/harry-kane-ankle-l.trail: There was plenty to learn from this year’s ceremony in London as Harry Kane took home the top honor

/football/2026/nov/20/harry-kane-ankle-l.headline: Harry Kane says wait to learn if he has won Ballon d’Or is stressful for family
/football/2026/nov/20/harry-kane-ankle-l.excerpt: Harry Kane would love to know now whether he has won the Ballon d’Or because the uncertainty and constant questions are driving his family to distraction. But the Bayern Munich and England striker accepts the suspense before the big reveal at the London Palladium on Monday night is part of the show. Kane is the odds-on favourite to win the prestigious individual honour after a prolific run of form. The 33-year-old scored 61 goals for Bayern last season and 12 for England. This time out, he has 10 for Bayern and six for England. He scored from the penalty spot in Wednesday’s 2-2 Champions League draw against Arsenal at the Allianz Arena, although his standout moment was the inch-perfect through ball that set up Alphonso Davies to make it 1-1. Barcelona’s Lamine Yamal is the second-favourite for the Ballon d’Or and Kylian Mbappé of Real Madrid is next in the betting. “I think my wife would prefer to know and my family … it’s very stressful for everyone,” Kane said. “I can see why they don’t tell people.
